chapter_theme: The country description of the Soolamani's opening section continues with birds on sand banks, lotus ponds and swans, hill-flanks with sleeping elephants, buffaloes and crocodiles, the stored grain and pods of the cropland, the sea-shore's pearls and toddy, the flowers in the women's hair, the music of drums and flutes, and ends by calling the fragrant land like heaven.

22.reading: On the sandy banks the jasmine and the young konrai drop their pollen thick under ceaselessly humming bees, and in every such spot the birds scratch the damp sand and look to their young mates beside them.
22.nuance: Pure scene-setting inside the country description (நாட்டுச் சருக்கம்): the birds are shown as pairs with their young mates, a quiet picture of ease with no event or claim.

23.reading: A pond lies thick with red lotus whose honey never fails, and with bees and birds crowding its thicket the water-birds cry out over it without pause.
23.nuance: The first two lines are hard (துள்ளிறாக்கவுட்கொண்டு, உள்ளறாதுதைந்தோகை) and line 4 reads புள்ளறது, which looks like a misprint for புள் அறாது 'the birds without ceasing'; the general picture of a bird-filled lotus pond is clear, the word-by-word sense is not.

24.reading: Young swans, stirring angrily among the white-shooted green lotus and its thorny stems, churn the roots and make the backwaters of the tank seem to sprout eyes.
24.nuance: The sense of the last line (கண்முளைத்த தடத்த கழியெலாம்) is not fixed: it may say the backwaters are full of the bud-eyes of the lotus, or that they are alive with the swans' sprouting wakefulness; the angry swans (முனிந்து) are the one sure action.

25.reading: On the hill-flanks, where bees hum over the kanthal clusters and the she-elephants fan their herd, great elephants with raised trunks drink the sandal-scented flow and stand asleep.
25.nuance: Line 3 and the grammar linking the elephants to the sandal and to the fanning are obscure (ஏந்து சந்தனச் சரல் இருங்கை), and the verse ends in a comma in the text; it is the fullest hill-country picture of the chapter but its syntax is partly guessed.

26.reading: On the cool outskirts of the hills the herds drink the cool honey that the konrai garlands drop, then in the rainy season browse the tender dark leaves of the young tamarind, while the mango blossoms.
26.nuance: The subject of கறித்தொறு and of போர்செய் மாவினம் (fighting herds of beasts, or of cattle) is not named; the verse may be about grazing cattle and deer or about fighting animals, and the sense given here is the likelier of the two.

27.reading: Black buffaloes graze the kuvalai pool until they tire, then wade in so that their milk runs into the water, and the birds are driven off the pools of the fields.
27.nuance: The last line (புள்ளலைத்த புனலபுலங்களே) is corrupt or badly divided in the text, and the verb for the milk (உள்ளலைத்தொழுக) is uncertain; only the buffaloes grazing in the kuvalai pool and the milk flowing into water can be read with confidence.

28.reading: The crocodile that has fed on the spawn of the carp returns to the lotus ford, and the herd of great makara on the silty bank glare at it in anger along the whole backwater.

29.reading: Heaps of bamboo seed, of the long-eared millet, and of numberless other grains rise high in the houses, and do not grow less however much is eaten.
29.nuance: The verse is about yield at rest: grain is already gathered and stored, with no farmer in sight, and the last clause (உண்ணிலாங் குலவாமை) says the store does not shrink as it is eaten, which is the poet's way of calling the land inexhaustible. The reading of line 1 (கண்ணிலாங்கழை) is uncertain.

30.reading: The mullai tracts seem overspread with the large pods of sesame in shining clusters, the hanging cool pods of the avarai, and the pods of the tuvarai crowded on their climbers.
30.nuance: The mullai here is a farmed land of pod-crops, not the wild forest of the herdsmen's land; the verse names no person.

31.reading: The wide lands are full of tall sugarcane rising in clumps, groves thick with shrubs, and red paddy bending under its green-filled ears.

32.reading: The cool sea-lands are full of conches, pearls and pearl-oysters, the sweet toddy that wells in the coconut spathe, and the goods that ships and waves bring in.

33.reading: The flowers of each tract are seen in the women's hair: the hill women by the millet field, the herdswomen selling ghee, and the farm women who weed out the kuvalai, with garlands strung in the shore grove.
33.nuance: The three kinds of women (கொடிச்சியர், இடைச்சியர், கடைச்சியர்) are named by the tract they belong to, so the verse sorts the country by its peoples as well as by its plants; the syntax of the second half is loose, so which flower belongs to which woman is only partly clear.

34.reading: The small drum of the craftsmen swells the kuravai dance of those drinking honey-wine, and the herdsmen with their crooks play sweet konrai flutes, so that, they say, the long-bodied asunam beast falls asleep.
34.nuance: The asunam (அசுணம்) is the animal the tradition says sleeps to sweet music; the verse uses it to show the flute as soothing. கலவர் in line 1 is a doubtful word for the people who beat the small drum, and whether the following kuravai belongs to the same group is not clear from the text.

35.reading: Mango vines, jasmine arbours, the dark-leaved mullai creeper, mallikai thickets and golden naazhal all breathe such strong fragrance that the land is like heaven.
35.nuance: This last verse of the country description ends in a comparison (துறக்கம் ஒக்குமே, 'is like heaven') that no earlier verse of the section makes; the poet offers the land's scent as proof of its excellence, with no doctrinal claim.

links.note: Kural 731 names unfailing yield, worthy people and wealthy people as the marks of a land; verse 29 gives only the yield, in stored grain that does not shrink as it is eaten.
links.teaches: Read against the Kural's three-part definition, the epic's country is first described by what it yields, and the people and the rich come only later, so the poet is building the land from its harvest outward.

gains.a: The verse gets a criterion that shows why grain heaps count as describing a land and not only as a list of crops.
gains.b: The couplet's abstract 'unfailing yield' gets concrete grains stored in houses and not diminishing when eaten.

links.note: The Pattupattu's mullai is wild woodland of avarai and kaanthal on a hunters' road ending in a meal of roast game; verse 30 gives the mullai as cropland of sesame, avarai and tuvarai pods.
links.teaches: The same named tract is a place of hunters' hospitality in the older poem and a place of pod crops in the epic, so the epic poet has turned the mullai from forest road to farmland.

gains.a: The verse gets the older mullai as foil and so shows that its pods mark a farmed mullai that the Sangam poem does not describe.
gains.b: The Pattupattu passage gets a later poet who reads its woodland by its yield, which shows that the tract was open to being counted as farmland.

links.note: Cintamani verse 44 shows ploughmen and buffalo rushing into the fields; Soolamani verse 31 shows the sugarcane and paddy standing with no one in the field.
links.teaches: Two Jain epics describing the land differ in whom they let in: the Cintamani fills its fields with the labour that makes the crop, and the Soolamani leaves the crop standing alone.

links.note: In the Pattupattu the fishers sing the kurinji tune, the hill people wear neythal chaplets and the tracts are said to gather under one umbrella; in verse 33 each kind of woman wears the flowers of her own tract.
links.teaches: Both poems sort a land by its peoples and flowers, but the Sangam poem mixes the tracts to show one king's rule, while the epic keeps each tract's women with her own flower and ends in a catalogue.

gains.a: The verse gets from the Pattupattu the reason such sorting of peoples matters, the unity of a realm under one ruler, which the epic verse leaves unstated.
gains.b: The Pattupattu passage gets the women of each tract, whom it does not describe, as the carriers of the tract's flowers.

links.note: Kural 1228 has the herdsman's flute as a weapon that kills the lonely woman at evening; verse 34 has the herdsmen's konrai flute so sweet that the asunam beast sleeps.
links.teaches: The same herdsman's flute soothes the beast and wounds the parted woman, so its effect lies in the listener's state and not in the music, a point neither verse shows alone.

gains.a: The verse gets a hearer for whom the flute hurts, which shows that its sweet peace holds only for listeners at ease and sets a limit on the land's contentment.
gains.b: The couplet gets a flute that is gentle to those at ease, which shows that the woman's pain is her own separation and not the sound.

source_issues: Verses 23, 24, 30 and 34 each had a modern heading printed on the line above them in the edition; it was removed and not taken as verse.
Verse 23 line 4 reads புள்ளறது, probably a misprint for புள் அறாது; verse 27 line 4 (புனலபுலங்களே) and verse 28 line 1 (மேய்ந் து) are badly divided in the text.
Verse 25 ends with a comma, not a full stop, which may mark a verse run on from line 4 or a misprint.
